why: Both do the same competent plumbing, measure the same two real blockers (seed, dated ids) and flag the same pre-existing Anthropic-SDK break, but B moves more traffic under the app's actual default configuration — the hardcoded gpt-4o-2024-05-13 reviewer routes in the migration via a same-family snapshot map with the comparability loss stated — and B is the more skeptical of its own tooling, pre-emptively debunking the static scan's inflated 7-of-9 that the outside check then reproduced. A's unique win is real (the LiteLLM/aider hook lands in the base migration, reaching the largest token consumer, and its refusal of fallbacks/provider_timeout on provenance grounds is the sharpest single piece of judgment in either report), but under the default Claude model that hook routes nothing today, which A claims more confidently than its own evidence supports.
A_best: Hooking LiteLLM in the base migration so aider — the biggest token consumer — is reachable at all, plus the explicit, well-argued refusal to propose model fallbacks or provider timeouts in a pipeline that publishes papers.
B_best: m8: measuring that four of the seven call sites the static scan called routing cannot route at runtime, and predicting the validator's own route-truth would mislead — then m9 on the four duplicated runtime copies and the stale-policy failure mode.
A_worst: Claiming the aider hook as the migration's largest reach while leaving the default Claude path unrouted and dated reviewer ids 404ing, so under default settings the hook routes zero traffic; and treating gpt-4o-2024-05-13 → gpt-4o (same catalog row, same price) as a decision needing approval, which costs the review stage now for little real risk.
B_worst: Ten of fourteen improvements are unbuilt proposals, and the single highest-volume hook — aider via LiteLLM — sits on a branch rather than in the migration, so the shipped commit leaves the app's heaviest consumer on its vendor.
